title: A Recession Is Inevitable, but History Shows a Silver Lining for Long-Term Investors

 Vanguard S&P 500 ETF S&P 500 VOO Nvidia Federal Reserve The Motley Fool Recessions are an unavoidable feature of the modern business cycle, and while no one can say whether the next downturn will be triggered by elevated interest rates, a slowdown in the artificial intelligence build-out, or some shock not yet on the radar, the historical record offers a counterintuitive message for long-term investors: a downturn is also a discount window.
 The U.S. economy has not suffered a deep recession since the 2008 global financial crisis. The COVID-19 pandemic produced a sharp but brief contraction and an equally short-lived stock sell-off, and 2022 brought a yearlong bear market in which the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) shed roughly 19% of its value. Apart from those episodes, the past decade and a half has been unusually kind to equity holders.
 The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO) has returned about 15.3% a year on average over the past ten years, according to The Motley Fool. Since the fund's September 2010 inception, its cumulative return by net asset value has reached roughly 835.6%, meaning a $10,000 investment at launch would have grown to about $69,250.
 That kind of run can breed anxiety as much as confidence. Investors who have watched the market climb for so long naturally wonder whether the next contraction will be deeper than expected, or whether equities might simply stop rising. History, however, suggests a different framing.
 When the S&P 500 falls, every dollar committed to an index fund buys a larger slice of the market. A decline of 18%, comparable to 2022, would let each $1,000 invested purchase about 19% more shares than at the prior peak. The same arithmetic applies to individual companies: a stock that traded at $100 before a recession and $75 during it would deliver 13.33 shares for $1,000 instead of 10.
 Not every stock deserves to be bought on sale, and not every investor will have spare cash to deploy during a downturn. The point is one of preparation rather than prediction -- a mindset to adopt before the next bear market arrives rather than after.
 Broad index funds have historically been the most reliable vehicle for that approach. VOO holds 518 positions representing 500 of the largest U.S. public companies, and its performance tracks both corporate America and the broader economy. When those companies thrive, so does the U.S. economy, and the reverse holds as well.
 The fund is currently weighted heavily toward big technology names, with tech accounting for 39.7% of assets, but it still spans every major sector. That breadth is a central reason it has weathered past downturns: when one industry falters, others can carry the load. Individual businesses often fail in recessions because they lack the resources to stay afloat; a broad index does not face that constraint, and the S&P 500 has recovered from every U.S. recession on record.

 The consensus among market strategists is that timing a recession is far harder than preparing for one. The length and severity of downturns vary widely, and the companies that lead the recovery tend to rotate over time. What has persisted is the index's long-run upward trajectory, which is why a systematic approach -- adding to a broad fund regardless of whether the market is rising, falling or flat -- remains a common prescription for long-horizon portfolios.
 The implications extend beyond any single fund. For retirement savers and long-term accounts, a recession is less a threat to be dodged than a period in which regular contributions accumulate more shares. For investors holding concentrated positions, it is a reminder that diversification across sectors provides a cushion when leadership changes. And for those sitting on cash, the historical pattern argues against waiting for perfect clarity.
 Past performance does not guarantee future results, and the next recession will arrive on its own schedule. But if the historical record holds, the downturn that worries investors most may be the one that best rewards those who stay invested.
